query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing controlled coherent nanoprecipitates in refractory high‐entropy alloys improves their high‐temperature mechanical strength and thermoelastic stability by facilitating smoother dislocation motion and limiting diffusion-based softening relative to a homogeneous single-phase alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy produced as a homogeneous, single-phase material (e.g., with a uniform BCC matrix).
generation.intervention: Processing modification (e.g., a tailored aging or heat-treatment cycle) to promote the formation of stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates within the alloy.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing (tensile, creep) conducted over a range from room temperature up to approximately 900 °C under controlled loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates and their interfaces with the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The nanoprecipitates act to relieve local stress concentrations and facilitate dislocation transmission, while also serving as barriers to lattice diffusion. This dual role reduces the rate of creep and thermal softening, thereby maintaining mechanical strength and stable thermoelastic properties at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline homogeneous alloy, the nanoprecipitate-containing alloy is predicted to exhibit a higher yield strength, enhanced ductility, reduced creep rates, and a more stable thermoelastic modulus during high-temperature operation.
generation.baseline: A refractory high-entropy alloy processed without the controlled induction of nanoprecipitates, maintaining a single-phase, homogeneous microstructure.
generation.boundary: Findings are expected to hold under high-temperature service conditions (up to 900 °C) and within the load regimes typical of high-temperature structural applications; effects may diminish if nanoprecipitate size/distribution is not adequately controlled.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in mechanical properties is uncertain, and the sensitivity of the effect to nanoprecipitate size, volume fraction, and spatial distribution needs to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same refractory high-entropy alloy composition. Process one set with a heat-treatment cycle that induces coherent nanoprecipitates and retain a homogeneous microstructure in the other set. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature tensile and creep tests, while concurrently using SEM/TEM to verify the microstructures.
measurements: Creep rate under constant stress at elevated temperatures
Thermoelastic modulus via dynamic mechanical analysis
Microstructural characterization (e.g., nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and coherence)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoprecipitate-containing alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength, creep resistance, or thermoelastic stability compared to the homogeneous alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures.

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
